explain.say: The plates float on the mantle, a thick layer of hot rock that is solid but can flow very slowly, like soft toffee, over millions of years.

explain.say: Heat from deep inside makes mantle rock rise, spread sideways and sink again in huge slow loops called convection currents. Under mid-ocean ridges, rising magma builds new plate.

explain.say: The biggest push actually comes where plates sink. Old ocean plate is cold and heavy, so it dives into the mantle and drags the rest of the plate behind it. This is called slab pull.

faq.a: Mantle convection is the very slow flow of hot rock in the mantle. Hotter rock rises, spreads out, cools and sinks again, carrying heat out of the Earth and helping move the plates.
asks: What are convection currents in the mantle?

faq.a: Slab pull is when an old, cold and dense ocean plate sinks into the mantle at a trench and pulls the rest of the plate along behind it. Scientists think it is the strongest force moving plates.

faq.q: How fast do tectonic plates move?
faq.a: Most plates move about 2 to 10 centimetres a year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow. Over millions of years that adds up to thousands of kilometres.
No, the mantle is almost all solid rock. But it is so hot and under so much pressure that it can flow very slowly over millions of years, like very stiff putty.
At mid-ocean ridges new plate is high and hot. As it cools it slides down and away from the ridge, pushing the plate outward. This is ridge push.
asks: How do mid-ocean ridges push plates?

facts: Most tectonic plates move between about 2 and 10 centimetres a year.
The Earth's mantle is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly over long times.
Slab pull, the sinking of old ocean plate, is thought to be the strongest force driving plate motion.

quiz.say: Which force do scientists think moves plates the most?
quiz.why: Old ocean plate is cold and dense, so it sinks into the mantle and drags the plate behind it.

wrong.1: The Moon raises tides but does not drive plates.
wrong.2: Ocean currents move water, not rock plates.
